title: Build a qualified position response
instructions: Use opinion or discursive writing only when the task asks for a position, evaluation or discussion. Practice prompt: Every secondary-school student should be required to complete one community-service project each term. Do you agree? Use this fictional school planning record: the current optional programme offers weekend litter collection, weekday reading support and on-campus resource sorting; the reading-support coordinator says irregular attendance makes pairing volunteers with younger readers difficult; some students travel long distances or care for siblings outside school; the proposed programme would let each student choose one bounded role and schedule; supervised on-campus roles and a genuine equivalent or exemption would be available for access or hardship needs. Do not treat the fictional record as real-world research. Answer all six questions before viewing feedback.

parts.prompt: Which controlling position answers the prompt most precisely and remains defensible from the fictional record?

options.text: Community service is good and every student should always do exactly the same project.
Schools should expect one bounded service contribution each term, provided students can choose accessible roles and use a genuine equivalent or exemption when circumstances require it.
There are arguments on both sides, so no judgement can be made.
Every required project will make every student caring and solve the community's problems, so schools should require the same weekend project from all students.

choice_rationales.A: This one-size-fits-all position ignores the access constraints in the record.
choice_rationales.B: The position answers the requirement question, gives a bounded scope and states the conditions needed for fairness.
choice_rationales.C: Acknowledging complexity does not remove the need to answer a prompt that asks for a judgement.
choice_rationales.D: The universal outcomes are unsupported by the fictional planning record.

parts.hint: Choose the position that answers the requirement question while defining the conditions that make it reasonable.
parts.correct_explanation: A qualified thesis can remain clear and arguable while accounting for a constraint that would otherwise weaken it.

parts.prompt: Which THREE details are most relevant to judging whether the requirement can be both dependable and accessible?

options.text: Irregular attendance makes it difficult to pair volunteers with younger readers.
Some students have long journeys or sibling-care duties outside school.
The proposal includes role choice, on-campus options and a genuine equivalent or exemption.
The school gate is painted dark green.
One student prefers basketball to reading.

choice_rationales.A: This detail identifies the dependability problem the proposal is meant to address.
choice_rationales.B: This detail identifies an access constraint that a fair design must answer.
choice_rationales.C: These protections show how the design could respond to different circumstances without requiring one identical activity.
choice_rationales.D: The gate colour has no bearing on the policy's dependability or accessibility.
choice_rationales.E: A single preference does not address the central design questions as directly as the access and scheduling evidence.

parts.hint: Select the current programme problem, the strongest access constraint and the design response.
parts.correct_explanation: Relevant support should illuminate both the reason for a proposal and the condition that keeps the writer's position defensible.

parts.prompt: Which paragraph develops the dependability reason through claim, detail, explanation and significance?

options.text: Required service is better. It is better because it is required. Everyone knows this.
The reading programme exists, and younger students read books. Community service has many forms.

A bounded term commitment could make participation more dependable than an unplanned invitation. In the fictional record, irregular attendance prevents the coordinator from preparing stable reading pairs; choosing a defined role and schedule would make the expected contribution visible. This supports a structured commitment, though it does not prove that every compulsory programme succeeds.

Required service is more dependable than an unplanned invitation. A research study proves that required service raises achievement by exactly 40 per cent in every school, and the fictional reading programme shows the same result. This proves that every compulsory programme succeeds, so schools should require service without any choices or exemptions.

choice_rationales.A: The circular assertion supplies neither evidence nor explanation.
choice_rationales.B: The details are listed without showing how they support a policy judgement.
choice_rationales.C: The paragraph states a bounded claim, uses a relevant record detail, explains the connection and limits what can be concluded.
choice_rationales.D: The statistic and universal research claim are invented and absent from the supplied record.

parts.hint: Look for a complete reasoning chain whose conclusion stays within the supplied fictional evidence.
parts.correct_explanation: Developed reasoning explains why a detail supports the claim and avoids enlarging a local example into an unsupported universal result.

parts.prompt: Which is the strongest relevant counterargument to the proposed requirement?

options.text: Anyone who disagrees must dislike the community.
A fixed external or weekend requirement could unfairly burden students with long journeys, caregiving duties or limited transport.
Some students may prefer a different colour for volunteer shirts.
Community service should be rejected because no policy can ever be perfect, and some students will always complain about it.

choice_rationales.A: This attacks imagined motives instead of presenting a critic's real concern.
choice_rationales.B: The objection identifies a concrete access problem that could make the requirement unfair unless the design changes.
choice_rationales.C: The shirt colour is peripheral to whether participation should be required.
choice_rationales.D: Demanding perfection would prevent reasonable evaluation of any policy.

parts.hint: Choose the objection that could reasonably change the design or strength of the position.
parts.correct_explanation: A fair counterargument tests the position against its strongest relevant constraint rather than an exaggerated or trivial alternative.

parts.prompt: Which concession-response paragraph addresses that counterargument without simply repeating or abandoning the position?

options.text: Travel and caregiving do not matter because service is important. Students with long journeys or family duties should simply organise their time better, so the original weekend-only external rule should remain unchanged for everyone without exceptions.
The access concern proves that schools should never organise any service programme.

A weekend-only external project could exclude students with travel or family responsibilities. The requirement would therefore need choices of time, supervised on-campus roles and a genuine equivalent or exemption; with those protections, one bounded contribution can still be a reasonable expectation.
There are two sides, and both are equally correct in every respect.

choice_rationales.A: This dismisses rather than answers the strongest concern.
choice_rationales.B: A flaw in one design does not establish that every possible programme must be rejected.
choice_rationales.C: The response concedes the valid access problem, changes the design and identifies the qualified position that remains.
choice_rationales.D: Complexity does not require the writer to avoid a reasoned judgement.

parts.hint: Acknowledge what is valid, show how it changes the proposal and state what judgement still holds.
parts.correct_explanation: Concession strengthens reasoning when it produces a more defensible position instead of a token contrast sentence.

parts.prompt: Which five-paragraph route would create the most focused response to the practice prompt?

options.text: Introduction: say service is good; paragraphs 2–4: repeat that service is good with different adjectives; conclusion: promise perfect results.

Introduction: state the qualified requirement; paragraph 2: explain how a defined role and schedule answer irregular participation; paragraph 3: explain how meaningful choice can preserve one expectation across different roles; paragraph 4: address travel and caregiving constraints through on-campus options and genuine alternatives; conclusion: retain the bounded expectation only under those fairness conditions.

Introduction: avoid taking a position; paragraph 2: list every possible service activity, from litter picking to reading; paragraph 3: invent statistics about how much students improve; paragraph 4: attack students who disagree with service; conclusion: introduce a new argument about whether school uniforms should change.
Introduction: copy the prompt; paragraph 2: discuss litter; paragraph 3: discuss books; paragraph 4: say both sides exist; conclusion: copy the prompt again.

choice_rationales.A: Repeated assertion does not develop distinct reasons or acknowledge the policy's relevant limit.
choice_rationales.B: Each paragraph performs a different job while preserving one qualified judgement across reasons, objection and conclusion.
choice_rationales.C: The route avoids evidence-bounded reasoning and changes topic at the end.
choice_rationales.D: Topic lists and repetition do not create a reasoned position or answer the strongest concern.

parts.hint: Choose the route with one qualified judgement, distinct developed reasons, a fair objection and a synthesising conclusion.
parts.correct_explanation: A coherent opinion or discursive response advances one judgement through distinct reasoning stages rather than repeating a preference or merely listing sides.
